subtitle: denn, doch, ja, mal: the tiny words that make you sound human
words.intro: Germany has more than a hundred publicly funded theatres, and a person in the audience is expected to have opinions. An evening at the theatre is a contact sport, played sitting down.

grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: These words have no real translation, and dictionaries give up on them. Linguists call them *Modalpartikeln*. Leave them out and your German will be correct and slightly frightening. Put them in and people will stop answering you in English.

grammar[1].blocks[0].rows[3][1]: Ich weiß nicht. Es war irgendwie interessant.
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: *Interessant* is what a polite German says when the evening was a mistake.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Softeners
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Say it to their face
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: Germans give direct feedback, and they don’t mean it unkindly. *Das war nicht gut* can come with a warm smile, from a friend. Your *Das war ziemlich interessant* may confuse them.
grammar[1].fact: A German phrase for a truly bad evening at the theatre is *Das war unter aller Kanone*: beneath all cannons. It probably began as a joke on Latin, *sub omni canone*: below every standard.

document.intro: A real playbill from the Vienna opera, for a Sunday in March 1900. Old type, old spelling (*Saalthüren*), but it’s exactly what you get today: who, when, how long, how much. Look at the lines between the two black hands.
document.fact: Gustav Mahler ran the Vienna opera at the time, and he was strict about latecomers: the doors stayed shut during the acts, as you can read on this bill. Theatres have kept the rule ever since.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Comment on the bill, with denn, doch, ja or mal.
reading.title: Faust, ohne Hose
reading.intro: Frau Huber has won two tickets to *Faust* at a very modern theatre. She takes Maya. The curtain rises on a bare stage with a large pig, a washing machine, and a Faust wearing nothing below the waist. There are five hours to go.
reading.fact: German directors are famous for what is known as *Regietheater*: the director’s ideas come first. Classics are performed with blood, water and the odd animal, and the audience boos loudly and comes back. Theatres are heavily subsidised, so tickets cost far less than the evening does.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with denn, doch, ja or mal, as in the text.
